name: Robot Air Hockey Challenge
ability_definition: The ability to time your movements or the movement of a piece of equipment in anticipation of changes in the speed and/or direction of a moving object or scene.

task_realism.reasoning: The tasks (Hit, Defend, Prepare) require a robot arm to time its motion to intercept a fast-moving puck whose direction changes after bounces. That is a direct instance of the core behavior Rate Control describes. It is a game setting rather than an industrial or vehicular one, but the demand of anticipating a moving object's trajectory and timing equipment movement to meet it is authentic and not abstracted.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Evaluation is closed-loop and real-time, with injected observation noise, tracking loss, and disturbances, which approximates real sensing imperfections. However, qualifying scoring happens in simulation on a single, well-structured table environment. There are no real-world stakes, no variety of settings, and limited physical sim-to-real effects in the scored results.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers interception, defense, and positioning against a moving object, which spans several facets of anticipatory timing. It is confined to planar puck dynamics on one table with one robot embodiment. It omits other workplace forms of rate control, such as matching conveyor speeds, vehicle or crane operation, and tracking changing scenes, as well as human-scale variability.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are continuous state observations (puck and joint positions). Outputs are low-level joint trajectories or commands executed in a physics loop. These closely resemble real control-system artifacts, with no multiple-choice or toy-grid abstraction. Success is judged by whether the timed movement actually works.

transferability_reasoning: The Robot Air Hockey Challenge directly exercises anticipatory timing of equipment movement against a fast, direction-changing object, using realistic continuous control formats and noisy, real-time closed-loop conditions. Transfer is limited by its single, narrow domain (planar puck interception on one simulated robot) and simulation-only scoring. It therefore captures a genuine but partial slice of workplace Rate Control.

2023.model_or_system: AiRLIHockey (MPC/optimal-control planner distilled via imitation learning)
2023.metric: mean success rate (%) over the hit, defend and prepare qualifying subtasks, evaluated in the organizers' modified (sim-to-real-perturbed) simulator
2023.human_reference: General adult workforce performing real-time interception and striking of moving objects (e.g., a typical adult playing casual air hockey, or an equipment operator timing movements to a moving target)

2024.model_or_system: AiRLIHockey (sampling-based MPC combined with a learned contact planner and behavioral-cloning distillation)
2024.metric: Qualifying-stage aggregate score on a 0-100 scale, based on success rates across the Hit, Defend and Prepare tasks
2024.human_reference: General adult workforce performing timed interception or rate-control tasks (e.g., equipment operators, casual air hockey or table-sport players). The analogy is a typical adult controlling an air hockey mallet directly.

2026.model_or_system: AiRLIHockey (hybrid: optimal-control/MPC policy distilled via imitation learning)
2026.metric: mean success rate (%) over the three qualifying sub-tasks (Hit, Defend, Prepare), simulated, 2023 protocol
2026.human_reference: General working-age adults performing everyday interception and timing tasks, with casual air-hockey play as the direct analogy. These are not trained robot teleoperators or competitive air-hockey players.
